overview.text: Astronomical distance describes how far a celestial object is from an observer and is fundamental to mapping the universe and determining objects’ intrinsic properties. Astronomers use the light-year—the distance light travels in a year—and the parsec, about 3.26 light-years. For nearby stars, parallax measures their apparent shift against background stars as Earth moves around the Sun: smaller shifts indicate greater distances. Beyond the reach of direct parallax, a calibrated “distance ladder” uses standard candles—objects whose known intrinsic brightness can be compared with how bright they appear. On cosmic scales, galaxy redshift interpreted through Hubble’s law also helps estimate distance, linking spectral shifts to the universe’s expansion.

key_facts.text: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year; one parsec equals about 3.26 light-years and corresponds to a parallax angle of one arcsecond.
As Earth orbits the Sun, nearby stars appear to shift against the distant background; the smaller the parallax, the farther the star.
A standard candle’s known intrinsic brightness can be compared with its apparent brightness to estimate its distance.
Cepheid variable stars are useful standard candles because their pulsation period is related to their luminosity.
Galaxy redshift measures shifts in spectral lines; interpreted with Hubble’s law, it can help estimate distance while reflecting the universe’s expansion.
